query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: High configurational entropy in near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles stabilizes their solid-solution structure at high service temperatures by suppressing elemental segregation and intermetallic phase formation.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles synthesized via physical or chemical methods, exhibiting a homogeneous, random distribution of constituent elements.
generation.intervention: Synthesize a comparative sample set with a deliberately skewed (non-equiatomic) composition that has lower configurational entropy, while keeping processing conditions and overall elemental types similar.
generation.conditions: Exposure to catalytic operation conditions at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric conditions at 473–1923 K.
generation.structural_mediator: The high mixing entropy and resulting homogeneous elemental distribution in the nanoparticles.
generation.mechanism: High mixing entropy increases the energetic barrier for phase separation and intermetallic compound formation. In equiatomic nanoparticles, this barrier preserves the random solid-solution structure even at elevated temperatures, whereas reduced entropy in non-equiatomic compositions facilitates elemental segregation or intermetallic phase nucleation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under high-temperature conditions, near-equiatomic nanoparticles will maintain their solid-solution structure and chemical homogeneity, while non-equiatomic nanoparticles will show measurable signs of phase segregation or the emergence of intermetallic phases, accompanied by changes in catalytic or thermoelectric properties.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles initially fabricated as near-equiatomic solid-solution materials exhibiting uniform phase distribution prior to thermal/operational treatment.
generation.boundary: The stabilization mechanism is expected to hold in inert or mildly reactive environments; extreme oxidative or corrosive conditions or significant size effects (e.g., very small nanoparticles) may introduce additional kinetics or surface energy factors that can compromise the predicted behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperatures at which transitional instabilities occur and the quantitative differences in phase separation behavior between equiatomic and non-equiatomic samples remain uncertain due to potential kinetic factors, nanoparticle size effects, and surface chemistry variations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sample sets: one with near-equiatomic composition (high configurational entropy) and one with intentionally non-equiatomic composition (lower configurational entropy). Expose both samples to identical high-temperature conditions corresponding to catalytic and thermoelectric service regimes. Use XRD and TEM combined with EDX mapping to assess phase stability, phase segregation, and chemical homogeneity after thermal treatment.
measurements: XRD phase analysis for detection of emerging intermetallic phases or phase separation
TEM imaging for morphological changes or particle coarsening
EDX elemental mapping to monitor chemical homogeneity
Surface area measurements to assess sintering effects
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the near-equiatomic nanoparticles exhibit comparable or enhanced phase segregation, intermetallic phase formation, or chemical inhomogeneity relative to the non-equiatomic control under identical high-temperature conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High entropy alloys (HEAs), complex concentrated alloys (CCAs), and multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) are the most common names of a new group of materials [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] ] introduced by Yeh et al. [ [6] ] and Cantor et al. [ [7] ] in the beginning of this century. Many definitions were proposed for such materials, but in general they consist of multiple (usually at least five) elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic composition [ [2] ]. This approach is different from the traditional alloy design using one (or maximum two) principal element and other minor elements. The presence of many elements in equiatomic (or near) composition leads to high mixing entropy and thus to many interesting properties [ [2] , [5] ]. One of such effects is the existence of a random solid solution and simple body centered cubic (bcc) or faced centered cubic (fcc) structure. Recently HEAs with hexagonal closed packed (hcp) structure have been reported as well [ [8] , [9] ]. A new approach to HEA design using the valence electron concentration (VEC) was recently proposed with the aim of increasing the plasticity of these alloys [ [10] , [11] ]. Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . However, despite the advantages of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, many issues arise owing to its low yield strength and costly and complex thermomechanical processing (i.e., multiple casting → hot rolling → homogenization → cold rolling → annealing → cutting, etc.
